newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan's Bhutto to take fight to court.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan's Bhutto to take fight to court.

text.p: Pakistan's ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto said on Monday she will lodge an appeal with the Supreme Court in the next two days asking that she be restored to power.
Bhutto told Reuters Television in an interview that she considered her sacking last week by President Farooq Leghari to be "a constitutional coup, a presidential coup and an act against democracy".
"I consider it to be illegal," she said, speaking at the prime minister's spacious official residence, which she said she would vacate on Tuesday.
"I shall go to the Supreme Court of Pakistan and I hope the Supreme Court will restore the National Assembly."
Bhutto said she planned to hold a meeting with lawyers on Monday. "I hope we can wrap it (the appeal) up. If we do, it will be filed tomorrow. Otherwise, the latest by the day after."

She said the legal petition would state that the allegations which Leghari levelled against her government were false, and that the ostensible aim of the presidential order -- to hold free, fair and impartial elections -- was also false.
Leghari's order dismissing Bhutto's government cited corruption, mismanagement and extra-judicial killings among other accusations which he said had virtually paralysed the government.

Bhutto, wearing a bright purple silk "shalwar kameez" and a beige head scarf, said she felt betrayed by Leghari, who once served in her cabinet and was handpicked by her to become president in 1993. She said he should step down.
"The president...should have first asked the prime minister for a vote of confidence," she said, claiming she had been a victim of a smear campaign.

Bhutto, 43, said she was confident the Supreme Court would rule as it did in 1993 when it overturned a presidential order sacking former prime minister Nawaz Sharif. Sharif was restored to power but later resigned under pressure.
Bhutto's legal challenge would be one of several which are expected to shift Pakistan's political crisis to the courts.

Interim Prime Minister Meraj Khalid told reporters on Sunday that his government was drawing up charges against Bhutto and her husband, Asif Ali Zardari. Asked if they would include criminal charges, he said: "All kinds of charges."
Khalid, who is a member of Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party (PPP) but distanced himself from her some time ago, did not spell out the charges but said they were expected this week.
He acknowledged they could include the alleged breach of human rights in Karachi, where some 375 people have been killed this year in ethnic and political strife.
The 43-year-old Bhutto is no stranger to courtroom battles. She was sacked in 1990 after 20 months in power and indicted on eight counts of abuse of power.
But courts cleared her of the charges, one by one, and she staged a comeback, winning re-election in 1993.
Bhutto's dismissal last week stirred no big protests or violence. Only small numbers of soldiers were deployed on the day she was removed from power, and they quickly returned to barracks.
Many citizens expressed relief her government had been sacked, citing inflation and widespread reports of corruption.
